Furthermore, in concert with the trend toward digital twins, this SEM will serve as the basis for an operational digital twin to provide a real-time digital representation of the system to monitor performance and adjust operational parameters in response to the dynamic changes in passenger demand patterns. The findings of the Phase III research make increasingly evident the challenges and complexities of AMD operational management as multiple AV fleets are combined with on-demand service using BEVs. Sam Lott Drawing from past simulation-based analytical studies over the past several decades of various ATN systems, Phase III recommends this SEM analysis approach for studying the principal variables that determine overall AMD network system performance. These principal variables include vehicle size(s), fleet size(s), vehicle storage/recharging locations, vehicle battery size, on-demand operations policies, and station configuration and operation. The SEM is well suited to study the impacts of passenger trip patterns and connections within the multimodal AMD network transport system, including time-of-day ridership fluctuations and regional transit intermodal station surge flows connecting to AMD circulator systems. Note that SEM includes consideration for not only the AMD AV modes but also all the accompanying pedestrian paths and associated activity, micromobility modes, regular vehicle modes, and complementary traditional transit services. This SEM shares similarities with the fixed-guideway ATN simulation studies that will be described through multiple examples in the next edition of the AMD implementation report series. One selected example of ATN simulation is the conceptual automated network system studied for the campus at California State University, Fresno (Figure 30). Each vehicle in the large operating fleet is dispatched in response to an individual passenger’s on-demand ride request to travel from a specific origin station to a specific destination station. Whereas this example is limited to the stations and network of the ATN system and the associated pedestrian activity throughout the campus, a SEM analysis would simulate not only the AV fleets but also all vehicles, passengers, and other road users; the movement of all modes (on demand and fixed route); the ride request and dispatch functions; and the energy subsystems of each EV fleet. This systems engineering approach is applicable in the early design phases, allowing trade-off analysis of cost and complexity to identify an optimal solution for the most critical elements of an AMD’s implementation.
